title: The king, the merchant and the sage
hookLine: a king without a kingdom and a merchant without a family sit in a forest and ask a sage the same question
carry: the goddess who binds the mind also frees it
tomorrow: is the goddess a second god, or the same one moving?

lines: WHY CAN'T THE MIND LET GO?
cards: A forest hermitage. A king sits on the ground; his ministers turned on him and his enemies took his city. Beside him sits a merchant whose own wife and sons threw him out for his money.
The strange part: the king keeps worrying about his old elephants and his treasury. The merchant keeps wondering whether his family is well. Both know these thoughts make no sense.
So they ask the sage: why can't the mind let go? That's where this year began. Today's summit sit goes back to that forest.

teach.h: A SUMMIT SIT: ONE STRETCH, SEEN FROM THE TOP.
teach.b: Near the top of the year, each day now looks back at one part of the climb. Start with the Devi Mahatmya.

teach.h: THE KING, THE MERCHANT AND THE SAGE.
teach.b: The king is Suratha, the merchant Samadhi, the sage Medhas, and his answer is the whole book.

teach.h: MAHAMAYA: THE POWER THAT BINDS IS THE POWER THAT FREES.
teach.b: The pull they feel, he says, is the goddess as Mahamaya, the great power that draws the minds of even the wise into confusion.

Then he tells them who she is, through her stories: the goddess leaving the sleeping Vishnu so that he wakes to face two demons; the goddess given every god's weapon to face the buffalo demon Mahisha; the goddess who meets Shumbha and Nishumbha, with Kali springing from her brow.
The same power that binds the mind, Medhas says, sets it free. The book ends not on a battlefield but by a river. They worship the goddess there, and she appears and asks what each wants.

teach.h: A KINGDOM BACK, OR A LOOSENED GRIP.
teach.b: The king asks for his kingdom back, and she grants it. The merchant asks for the knowledge that loosens the grip of me and mine. She grants that too.
Same question, two different answers. That's the Shakta teaching in one line: the pull of me and mine, maya, isn't outside the goddess. It is her power, so the way out runs through her too.
And the question is an ordinary one: why does my mind keep going back to what hurt me? The book doesn't scold it. It sends you to the Mother, who holds the knot and its loosening.

how: Some devotees of the goddess recite the Devi Mahatmya in full, in one sitting or spread across the nights of Navaratri.

o: a final exam on everything taught this year
a long silent retreat held at a mountain temple
a stop near the year's top to look back at one stretch

games.q: the frame of the Devi Mahatmya — tap the pairs.
p: a king who lost his kingdom
a merchant driven out by his family
the sage who tells her stories
the power that binds and frees the mind

s: the Devi Mahatmya ends on the battlefield
it ends by a river, where the goddess asks the king and the merchant what each wants.
the king and the merchant ask the goddess for the same thing
the king asks for his kingdom back; the merchant asks for the knowledge that loosens me and mine.
in the book, the power that confuses the mind is also the power that frees it
Medhas says it is the same goddess, Mahamaya, who binds and who sets free.

games.q: you're the merchant, by the river. the goddess asks what you want. your family threw you out for your money. what do you ask for?
o: your house and your money back.
the knowledge that loosens me and mine.
games.why: the merchant asks for the knowledge that frees him from clinging, and the goddess grants it. the king, beside him, asks for his kingdom, and gets that too.

practice: Notice one thing your mind keeps going back to, as the king went back to his elephants, and without arguing or following, name it once and let it sit beside you.
Each time it pulls, come back to the breath; if you pray, hold it up to the goddess, or to God, as the two did by the river.
